questions.question: Define human rights and explain why World War II led to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
questions.expected_answer: Human rights: basic rights and freedoms belonging to every person because they are human; universal and inherent; governments must respect and protect them. Earlier ideas (ubuntu, 1689, 1776, 1789) often excluded many. WWII: about 70-85 million dead, mostly civilians; Holocaust (about 6 million Jews and others) carried out through laws such as the Nuremberg Laws 1935; abuses by Japan. Post-war view that treatment of citizens is an international concern; Nuremberg trials and crimes against humanity; UN Charter 1945 reaffirmed faith in human rights.

questions.question: Describe how the Declaration was drafted and adopted and summarise its main rights.
questions.expected_answer: UN founded 24 October 1945 (Charter 26 June 1945, Smuts helped draft preamble). Commission on Human Rights chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt; Cassin, P.C. Chang, Malik, Humphrey, Hansa Mehta. Adopted 10 December 1948 in Paris: 48 for, 0 against, 8 abstentions (USSR and 5 communist states, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). 30 articles: Art 1 free and equal; Art 2 non-discrimination; civil (life, no slavery, no torture, equality before law, no arbitrary arrest, fair trial); political (thought, expression, assembly, Art 21 participation and elections); movement, asylum, nationality, marriage; economic/social (work, standard of living, Art 26 education). Not binding; 1966 covenants.

questions.question: Explain the contrast between the Declaration and apartheid, and its influence on South Africa's Bill of Rights.
questions.expected_answer: 26 May 1948 NP (Malan) won whites-only election and began apartheid; SA abstained. Contradictions: Population Registration Act vs Art 2, pass laws vs Art 13, Mixed Marriages Act vs Art 16, detention without trial vs Arts 9-10, no vote vs Art 21, Bantu Education vs Art 26. Used by liberation movements (African Claims 1943, Freedom Charter 1955); UN declared apartheid a crime against humanity in 1973. 1996 Constitution Chapter 2 Bill of Rights: binding, detailed equality clause, enforceable socio-economic rights; Human Rights Day 21 March (Sharpeville 1960).
